opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important ideas for anyone thinking about AI safety, even if Wolfram didn't frame it that way. The core insight is that for a lot of systems, even very simple ones like cellular automata with a few rules, there is no shortcut. You can't predict what the system will do at step one million without actually running all one million steps. The computation itself is the fastest way to find out the answer.

Now apply that to a superintelligent system. People say, "We'll just analyze it, we'll verify it, we'll predict its behavior before we deploy it." But if a system that simple is already computationally irreducible, what hope do we have with something orders of magnitude more complex than us? To know what it will do, you basically have to let it do it. And by then, in the safety context, it may be too late. You only get one chance to get it right.

It also connects to a lot of the impossibility results I've been collecting: unpredictability, unexplainability, incomprehensibility. A smarter agent, by definition, will make decisions you couldn't have made yourself. If you could predict every move it makes, you'd be as smart as it is. So irreducibility is kind of the formal backbone for that intuition: complexity doesn't compress, and you can't summarize the future of a system smarter than you into something you can check in advance.

And there's a humbling side to it. We like to think science gives us a way to jump ahead of nature, compute the answer with an equation. Wolfram shows that's the exception, little pockets of reducibility in a mostly irreducible universe. So when someone tells me they have a guaranteed way to control a system that's far more capable than humanity, my question is: where's the shortcut? Because the math suggests there usually isn't one.

r001.rationale: It says there is no shortcut to predicting the system’s behavior and that you must run all one million steps to find out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think computational irreducibility is one of the most important ideas for anyone who wants to understand complex systems, and especially intelligent systems. What Wolfram showed, with his cellular automata and other simple programs, is that there are systems where the only way to find out what they will do is to actually run them. There is no shortcut. You cannot write down a formula that tells you the state at step one million without going through all the intermediate steps.

That has very deep implications for what I work on, which is AI safety. We want to predict what an advanced AI system will do. We want to prove it is safe. But if the system is computationally irreducible, and I would argue that any system of general intelligence is, then prediction in the strong sense becomes impossible. You cannot simulate it faster than it runs itself. And if you could simulate it perfectly, you would essentially have another copy of the same system, with the same problems.

So this connects to a lot of impossibility results. I have a paper on unpredictability of AI, another on unexplainability, and these all follow from the same logic. If a system is smarter than you, and it is irreducible, you cannot know in advance what it will decide. You can only find out after the fact. And with sufficiently capable systems, after the fact may be too late.

People sometimes push back and say, well, we test software all the time, we do verification. But verification works on systems that are reducible, where you can enumerate states or prove properties formally. Complex systems like weather, like economies, like brains, like large neural networks, those resist this. Even today we do not fully understand why a trained model gives a particular output. Interpretability is still very limited. And as capability goes up, the gap between what the system can do and what we can explain about it keeps growing.

So I find Wolfram's framing useful because it gives a mathematical basis for a kind of humility. It is not that we are not clever enough yet. It is that for certain systems, there is a fundamental limit on how much you can know in advance. And I think that should change how we think about building things that are more capable than we are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the only way to find out what such a system will do is to run it, with no shortcut around the intermediate steps.

astra-6.text:
Because it tells us that even if you know the rules of a system, you may not be able to predict what it will do without actually running it. The rules can be very simple, but the behavior they produce can be extraordinarily complex. And there may be no shortcut to finding out what happens a million steps from now—you have to go through those steps.

For AI safety, that's a serious problem. We would like to examine a system and say, before we deploy it, “Here is how it will behave in every situation.” Computational irreducibility suggests there are limits to our ability to do that. A complete description of the program doesn't necessarily give you a practical way to anticipate its behavior.

That doesn't mean we can't predict anything or prove particular properties. But it challenges the assumption that enough intelligence or enough analysis will let us predict everything about a complex system.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be no shortcut to predicting what happens later and that you have to run through the steps.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that, for some systems, there is no shortcut to finding out what they’re going to do. Even if you know the rules and the initial conditions, you may have to run the system, step by step, to see the outcome. A very simple program can produce behavior that is extraordinarily difficult to predict.

That’s relevant to AI because we often assume that if we built a system, we should be able to understand and predict it. But knowing the code is not the same as knowing everything that code will do. If predicting an AI’s behavior requires running it, then a simulation may reveal a dangerous action only when the simulated system actually takes that action.

That doesn’t mean we can’t predict anything or establish useful constraints. But it puts limits on the idea that we can examine an arbitrarily complex system in advance and guarantee all of its future behavior. For AI safety, that distinction is very important.

r001.rationale: The response says that for some systems there is no shortcut to knowing the outcome and that you may have to run the system step by step, which conveys that predicting its behavior requires following its evolution.
